title: JavaScript function forms, parameters, and return behavior
concepts: Functions as callable objects and first-class values
How function syntax affects name binding and this
How argument values initialize formal parameters
How return completion differs from fall-through
How recursion and higher-order functions compose
accuracyFacts: Default parameter initializers run at call time only when the argument is absent or explicitly undefined; null does not trigger the default. Initializers are evaluated left-to-right in a parameter environment, and later parameters are not yet initialized when an earlier initializer references them.

A parameter list with defaults, rest, or destructuring is non-simple. Non-strict ordinary functions have a mapped arguments object only with a simple parameter list; strict functions use unmapped arguments. Arrow functions have no own arguments binding and resolve an outer one if present.

The arguments object is array-like, not an Array. Its length is the number of actual arguments supplied. Rest parameters create a real Array of the remaining arguments and are usually clearer; arguments.callee is deprecated and forbidden in strict mode.

Arrow functions have lexical this, super, and new.target behavior, no own arguments, and cannot be used as constructors. Ordinary concise methods are also non-constructible, but unlike arrows they have dynamic this and a home object for super.

Async functions always return a Promise: normal return values fulfill it and thrown exceptions reject it. Generator calls return a suspended generator object without running the body immediately; async generator calls return an async generator object. Scheduling and full protocol semantics are covered in the Promise and iteration lessons.

The Function constructor dynamically parses parameter/body strings and creates a function that closes over the global environment rather than the local lexical scope where the constructor call appears. Treat it like dynamic code evaluation; it is a security and optimization hazard and may be blocked by Content Security Policy.

Function length is descriptive expected-argument metadata: the count stops before the first default-initialized or rest parameter. It does not restrict calls. Function names may be inferred from syntactic context and have no semantic identity value.

A return statement with no expression and falling off the end of a function both produce undefined. A line terminator after return ends the return statement; place the expression on the same line or use parentheses/braces clearly.

A function declaration creates a binding according to its containing scope; block-level and Annex B web-legacy rules make blanket claims that every declaration is hoisted everywhere inaccurate. Named function expressions have an internal self-name binding scoped to the expression.
